description: Brali Deep Run wave 3, 2026-09-11. Three additional low-complexity mechanisms completed source review: context-sensitive micro-conversations during routine exchanges, the consider-the-opposite debiasing check, and temptation bundling for delayed-benefit behavior. The debiasing protocol is deliberately bounded by both the classic strategy experiment and a 2025 randomized-trial meta-analysis showing only a small average effect and uncertain real-world transfer.

genuine-micro-conversation.note: Reviewed against the complete field-experiment report. Public guidance is limited to making an already-occurring low-pressure interaction slightly more social when the other person appears willing. It does not claim loneliness treatment, social-anxiety treatment, or benefits in contexts where conversation is intrusive or impractical.

consider-the-opposite.note: Reviewed against the complete classic consider-the-opposite experiments and a 2025 meta-analysis of educational debiasing RCTs. The strategy is presented as a bounded check against one-sided reasoning, not a general immunity to cognitive bias or proof of real-world transfer.

temptation-bundling.note: Reviewed against the original randomized gym field experiment and a later large exercise field experiment. Public guidance keeps the strongest evidence tied to compatible rewards and exercise/task initiation, makes effect decay explicit, and does not generalize the method to every habit.

genuine-micro-conversation.reason: The protocol concerns small context-sensitive social interactions and low-pressure initiation rather than conflict repair or formal communication training.

consider-the-opposite.reason: The action is a structured debiasing check used while evaluating evidence and judgments, directly connecting decision-making, cognitive-bias awareness and critical thinking.

temptation-bundling.reason: The method adds an immediate reward to a delayed-benefit action. Field evidence is strongest for exercise, while the reusable mechanism concerns starting and repeating beneficial behavior.

research_candidates.title: Is Efficiency Overrated?: Minimal Social Interactions Lead to Belonging and Positive Affect
research_candidates.review_notes: Complete author-uploaded article reviewed alongside the journal record. Sixty people approaching a busy urban Starbucks were randomly assigned to make the barista interaction social or efficient. A research assistant blind to condition collected post-interaction measures. The social condition involved smiling, eye contact and brief conversation and produced higher positive affect, lower negative affect, greater satisfaction and greater belonging. The authors explicitly note that effects may be limited to contexts where service providers are willing and able to engage and may not generalize to pressured contexts. Outcomes were immediate and self-reported; the experiment does not establish durable social connection or treatment effects.

research_candidates.title: Considering the opposite: A corrective strategy for social judgment
research_candidates.container_title: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
research_candidates.review_notes: Complete article reviewed through an available full-text copy and checked against the PubMed/APA record. Across two experiments totaling 150 undergraduates, consider-the-opposite instructions or materials reduced biased assimilation and biased hypothesis testing more than generic instructions to be fair and unbiased. The authors also note circumstances where considering the opposite could itself overweight disconfirming information. The experiments are classic task-specific social-judgment evidence, not proof of durable or domain-general debiasing.

research_candidates.title: Systematic review and meta-analysis of educational approaches to reduce cognitive biases among students
research_candidates.review_notes: Full author-provided article and publisher record reviewed. The systematic review identified 54 randomized controlled trials with 383 effect sizes and 10,941 participants; the main meta-analysis of 160 effects from 41 studies found a small average reduction in targeted biases (g 0.26, 95% CI 0.14 to 0.39). Many interventions used cognitive strategies including consider-the-opposite and feedback. All included studies had unclear or high risk of bias, some publication-bias risk was present, and the authors explicitly highlight uncertainty about depth and transfer beyond trained tasks. The review supports modest expectations for debiasing training and argues against broad real-world claims.

research_candidates.title: Teaching temptation bundling to boost exercise: A field experiment
research_candidates.container_title: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes
research_candidates.review_notes: Full open article reviewed. A large gym-based StepUp program tested free audiobooks with and without explicit temptation-bundling encouragement and also compared those groups with a no-audiobook control. The preregistered randomized comparison included 2,334 eligible gym members; a broader comparison included 6,792 members. Explicit teaching added only a modest incremental effect over receiving the audiobook alone, while audiobook-plus-encouragement versus control increased weekly workout likelihood and gym visits by roughly 10-14%/10-12% in reported analyses, with some effects persisting after the intervention. The evidence remains exercise-specific and bundled with other StepUp components such as planning, reminders and small rewards. The original university field experiment also found strong initial effects that decayed over time and after a holiday disruption.

evidence_decisions.source_title: Is Efficiency Overrated?: Minimal Social Interactions Lead to Belonging and Positive Affect
evidence_decisions.citation_text: Sandstrom GM, Dunn EW. Soc Psychol Personal Sci. 2014;5(4):437-442.
evidence_decisions.study_design: Randomized real-world field experiment at a busy urban coffee shop. Participants were assigned to make an already-required cashier interaction either social or maximally efficient; a research assistant blind to condition collected immediate outcomes after the purchase.
evidence_decisions.population: 60 adult coffee-shop customers recruited in person from a busy urban shopping district, spanning multiple adult age groups.
evidence_decisions.intervention_or_exposure: A brief social service interaction involving smiling, eye contact and conversation versus an efficient transaction with unnecessary conversation avoided.
evidence_decisions.supported_claim: In a low-pressure context where interaction is already occurring and the other person is able to engage, adding a brief genuine social exchange can improve immediate affect, satisfaction and belonging relative to treating the exchange as purely efficient. Brali can offer this as a context-sensitive social micro-practice, not a loneliness or mental-health intervention.
unsupported_or_overstated_claims: Brief stranger conversations treat loneliness or social anxiety.
Everyone benefits from talking to strangers.
Service workers should be expected to provide conversation.
The effect generalizes to rushed, unsafe, high-pressure, culturally inappropriate or unwanted interactions.
One brief interaction produces durable relationship or wellbeing changes.
limitations: Small single-site sample of 60 participants.
Immediate self-reported outcomes rather than long-term behavior or wellbeing.
The context was a coffee shop where friendly customer interaction was normal.
Participants could infer the social purpose of the manipulation, creating possible demand characteristics.
The authors explicitly warn that other service contexts may not support the same kind of interaction.
evidence_decisions.notes: Publish with an explicit willingness/context gate. The action is an optional extension of an existing exchange, not a quota of strangers or a treatment claim.

evidence_decisions.source_title: Considering the opposite: A corrective strategy for social judgment
evidence_decisions.citation_text: Lord CG, Lepper MR, Preston E. J Pers Soc Psychol. 1984;47(6):1231-1243.
evidence_decisions.study_design: Two conceptually parallel experiments manipulating whether participants considered possibilities opposed to their current beliefs or impressions, compared with alternative instructions including generic fairness/unbiasedness prompts.
evidence_decisions.intervention_or_exposure: Explicit consider-the-opposite instructions or materials designed to make opposite possibilities salient during evaluation of ambiguous evidence and hypothesis testing about personality impressions.
outcomes: Biased hypothesis testing in social judgment
evidence_decisions.supported_claim: When a judgment is vulnerable to one-sided evidence processing, deliberately generating an opposed possibility can reduce bias on some tasks more effectively than simply telling oneself to be fair or unbiased. Brali can use this as a concrete pre-decision check while preserving the possibility that the original conclusion remains correct.
unsupported_or_overstated_claims: Consider-the-opposite eliminates confirmation bias.
The technique transfers automatically to every real-world decision.
The opposite conclusion should be preferred once generated.
More counterarguments are always better.
The strategy should be used for every trivial or reversible choice.
limitations: Classic laboratory/social-judgment evidence from undergraduate samples.
Only two focal task domains were tested in the original article.
Long-term persistence and broad transfer were not established.
The authors note that considering the opposite can in some circumstances overweight disconfirming evidence and create a different form of partiality.
Demand characteristics and task-specific effects remain possible.
evidence_decisions.notes: Publish as a single structured alternative-generation step followed by a discriminating-evidence question. Do not tell users to reverse their decision by default.

evidence_decisions.source_title: Systematic review and meta-analysis of educational approaches to reduce cognitive biases among students
evidence_decisions.citation_text: Swaryandini G, Graham J, Griffith S, et al. Nat Hum Behav. 2025;9:2510-2538.
evidence_decisions.study_design: Systematic review of 54 randomized controlled trials with 383 effect sizes and meta-analysis of 160 effects from 41 studies evaluating educational interventions intended to reduce cognitive biases.
evidence_decisions.population: 10,941 participants across the randomized studies, primarily students in educational settings and spanning multiple targeted cognitive biases.
evidence_decisions.intervention_or_exposure: Educational debiasing approaches including cognitive strategies, feedback, games, instructional materials and multi-component training; some included consider-the-opposite components.
outcomes: Evidence about retention and transfer where reported
evidence_decisions.supported_claim: Debiasing education can produce a small average improvement on targeted bias tasks. This supports modest expectations for a consider-the-opposite check while making the boundary explicit: depth of learning and transfer to meaningful real-world decisions remain uncertain.
unsupported_or_overstated_claims: A brief consider-the-opposite prompt has a meta-analytically proven effect size of g 0.26.
Debiasing training reliably transfers to professional and personal decisions.
All cognitive biases respond similarly to training.
One educational strategy was established as universally best.
A small targeted-task effect implies large practical decision improvements.
limitations: All included studies were rated unclear or high risk of bias.
There was some evidence of publication bias.
Interventions, bias targets and outcome measures were highly heterogeneous.
Transfer beyond explicitly trained tasks was limited or uncertain in many studies.
The pooled effect represents diverse educational interventions rather than the consider-the-opposite strategy alone.
evidence_decisions.notes: Use as a calibration source: the direction is encouraging, the average effect is small, and real-world transfer must remain an open question.

evidence_decisions.source_title: Teaching temptation bundling to boost exercise: A field experiment
evidence_decisions.citation_text: Milkman KL, Duckworth AL, Choi J, Laibson D, Madrian B. Organ Behav Hum Decis Process. 2020.
evidence_decisions.study_design: Large real-world gym field program containing a preregistered randomized comparison of a free audiobook plus temptation-bundling instruction versus a free audiobook alone, plus a broader comparison with a no-audiobook control. Objective gym check-in data were used before, during and after the intervention.
evidence_decisions.population: Adult members of 24 Hour Fitness who enrolled in a four-week exercise-boosting program. The preregistered eligible comparison included 2,334 participants; the broader three-condition analysis included 6,792 participants.
evidence_decisions.intervention_or_exposure: A free audiobook paired with explicit instruction and reminders to reserve desired media for gym exercise, compared with audiobook-only and no-audiobook program conditions. All StepUp participants also encountered planning prompts, reminders and small visit-linked rewards.
outcomes: Probability of at least one weekly gym workout
Average weekly gym visits during the program
evidence_decisions.supported_claim: Pairing a delayed-benefit behavior with a compatible immediate reward can modestly increase exercise participation in some field settings. Brali can offer temptation bundling as a task-initiation experiment, while keeping its strongest empirical anchor in exercise and requiring that the reward not impair the useful activity.
unsupported_or_overstated_claims: Temptation bundling works equally well for every habit.
The audiobook itself proves the mechanism independent of planning, reminders and other program components.
A reward should always be restricted exclusively to the target behavior.
The technique reliably creates permanent habits.
Adding entertainment is appropriate for driving, complex learning, technical work or exercise where divided attention creates risk.
limitations: The strongest evidence is concentrated in exercise/gym behavior rather than arbitrary habits.
The large StepUp program included multiple behavior-change components, complicating attribution in broader control comparisons.
The incremental effect of explicit temptation-bundling teaching over receiving the audiobook alone was modest.
Participants self-selected into an exercise-boosting program and may have been more motivated than typical gym members.
The original field experiment showed that effects can decay and be disrupted by context changes such as holidays.
evidence_decisions.notes: Publish with a compatibility/safety gate and behavior tracking. Keep generalization from exercise to other low-complexity habits explicitly tentative.
